title: wsutil: Add a lookup of the processes that have a socket open
description:
Fourth of the series adding capture-time process attribution (design on wireshark-dev: https://lists.wireshark.org/archives/wireshark-dev/202609/msg00002.html; see #17525 and #1184; previous MRs: !26470, !26471, !26479).

The file format (!26471) and the display (!26479) are in place; this MR adds the piece that will let dumpcap fill the blocks: a small libwsutil API that maps a socket to the processes that have it open, using only what each operating system offers to an unprivileged process. Nothing uses it yet, so it can be reviewed on its own for portability and style; the dumpcap option is the next MR.

**API** (`wsutil/process_lookup.h`)

- `ws_process_lookup_new()` / `_free()`: a lookup context holding a snapshot of the OS socket tables and a cache of process records.
- `ws_process_lookup_socket(lookup, protocol, local, remote, processes)`: appends every process that has the TCP or UDP socket with that local endpoint and, if connected, remote endpoint open, and returns how many. If nothing matches both ends, a socket bound to the local endpoint alone is tried (listening, or unconnected UDP), then one bound to the port on any address, of either IP version. A miss refreshes the snapshot, but not more often than a configurable interval (default 250 ms, `ws_process_lookup_set_refresh_interval()`), which bounds the cost of packets that belong to no local socket. Several processes can have one socket open (inherited across `fork()`, or passed between processes), and several sockets can match (SO_REUSEPORT); all of them are reported, the process that has had the socket open longest first, normally the one that created it, which is the order dumpcap will write the `epb_processid_threadid` options in now that the draft allows one per process. Windows itself reports one process per socket, the one that bound it.
- `ws_process_lookup_pid()`: a process by ID.
- `ws_process_info_t`: pid, parent, uid, name, path, command line (NUL-separated arguments), user name, start time, the attributes of the process information block. Records are owned by the context and stay valid until it is freed; when a process ID is reused, the start time tells the two apart and both records are kept.

**Backends**, chosen in `wsutil/CMakeLists.txt`:

- Windows: `GetExtendedTcpTable()` / `GetExtendedUdpTable()` with owning PIDs (both IP versions), a Toolhelp snapshot for every process's name and parent, `QueryFullProcessImageNameW()` / `GetProcessTimes()` / the token's SID for path, start time and user, and the command line from the process's PEB via `ReadProcessMemory()` (own processes; `NtQueryInformationProcess` is resolved at run time and only public `winternl.h` structures are used). No new link libraries.
- Linux: `/proc/net/{tcp,udp}{,6}` for the sockets and their inodes, `/proc/<pid>/fd` to map inodes to processes (own processes unprivileged; everybody's with CAP_SYS_PTRACE or as root), and `/proc/<pid>/{stat,comm,exe,cmdline,status}` for the details. Kept to `/proc` rather than `NETLINK_SOCK_DIAG` so it needs no kernel headers or libnl; sock_diag can replace the socket enumeration later if the text tables turn out too slow on very busy hosts.
- Everything else: a stub; `ws_process_lookup_supported()` is false and `ws_process_lookup_new()` explains. macOS is deliberately not in this MR: the unprivileged socket table with process IDs (`net.inet.tcp.pcblist_n`) is only declared in xnu's private headers, and `libproc` covers the caller's own processes only; I would rather add it in its own MR with a Mac to test on than ship it untested.

**Tests**: `test_wsutil` gains three tests that create loopback sockets and look the test process up: a TCP connection seen from both ends and its listener, a listener bound to any address matched through the wildcard fallback, an unconnected UDP socket with and without a caller-supplied remote end, a protocol mismatch, an IPv6 listener (skipped without IPv6 loopback), a nonexistent PID, the sockets after closing (a TIME_WAIT socket has no owner), and on Unix a listener inherited by a forked child, reported for both with the parent first, and for the child alone once the parent closes it. Each checks the record describes the test executable (pid, name, path, command line, user, start time, and on Unix the uid).

Built and tested on Windows (MSVC) and, in the CI container image, on Linux with the GCC, Clang + code checks and ASAN jobs.

notes.body: What if a given socket is open in more than one process?

Hi guy, I've discussed this with Fable 5.1, and this is the current thinking:

Both the API and the file format carry one process per packet (option 8 holds a single PID), so the lookup has to pick one.

On Windows the system picks: `GetExtendedTcpTable()`/`GetExtendedUdpTable()` report one owning process per endpoint, the one that bound it, and that is what is returned.

On Linux, the first version kept whichever process the `/proc` scan happened to visit last, which was arbitrary. I've changed it so that a socket that several processes have open (inherited across `fork()`, or passed with `SCM_RIGHTS`) is attributed to the process that has had it open longest, i.e. the earliest-started of them, normally the one that created it, with the lower PID breaking ties within a clock tick. The rule is documented in `process_lookup.h`, and there's a new unit test that forks a child holding a listening socket and checks that the parent is reported, and the child once the parent has closed its copy.

In practice, for a pre-fork server that means the listening socket is attributed to the master process, while each accepted connection is attributed to the worker that accepted it, since that socket only exists there.

It is a rule, not an answer for every case: with socket activation the oldest holder of a listener is systemd or launchd rather than the service, a privilege-separated daemon like sshd keeps the connection in both the root monitor and the unprivileged child that does the I/O, and with SO_REUSEPORT several processes have their own socket on the same port and the socket table cannot say which one got a given datagram. The table can only ever say who holds a socket; saying who sent or received a particular packet needs packet-level attribution (eBPF, ETW, PKTAP), which is the deferred "exact" mode. Since the process information blocks carry the parent PID, dumpcap can also write a block for every holder of a shared socket so the relationship is visible in the file even though each packet names one process; I intend to do that in the dumpcap MR.

Nice one, thanks Guy. It's our own API (wsutil/process_lookup.h) in this MR, so yes. I'll change it to return every process holding a matching socket, oldest first, so the first entry is normally the one that created the socket, and update the tests. +/** @file
+ *
+ * Look up the processes that have a network socket open, from the
+ * operating system's socket tables, and describe them.
+ *
+ * Wireshark - Network traffic analyzer
+ * By Gerald Combs <gerald@wireshark.org>
+ * Copyright 1998 Gerald Combs
+ *
+ * SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0-or-later
+ */
+
+#ifndef __WSUTIL_PROCESS_LOOKUP_H__
+#define __WSUTIL_PROCESS_LOOKUP_H__
+
+#include <wireshark.h>
+#include <wsutil/inet_addr.h>
+
+#ifdef __cplusplus
+extern "C" {
+#endif /* __cplusplus */
+
+/**
+ * @brief What the operating system knows about a process.
+ *
+ * Whatever the operating system does not provide, or does not let the
+ * calling user see, is NULL (strings), 0 (the start time) or flagged as
+ * absent. Strings are UTF-8.
+ */
+typedef struct ws_process_info {
+    uint32_t  pid;            /**< The process ID. */
+    bool      has_ppid;       /**< Whether ppid is known. */
+    uint32_t  ppid;           /**< The ID of the parent process. */
+    bool      has_uid;        /**< Whether uid is known (systems with numeric user IDs). */
+    uint32_t  uid;            /**< The numeric ID of the user the process runs as. */
+    char     *name;           /**< The short name of the process, typically its executable's file name, or NULL. */
+    char     *path;           /**< The full path of the executable image, or NULL. */
+    char     *user;           /**< The name of the user the process runs as, e.g. "alice" or "DOMAIN\\alice", or NULL. */
+    uint8_t  *cmdline;        /**< The command line, its arguments separated by NULs (none after the last), or NULL. */
+    size_t    cmdline_len;    /**< The length of cmdline, in bytes. */
+    uint64_t  start_time_ns;  /**< When the process started, in nanoseconds since the Epoch, or 0 if unknown. */
+} ws_process_info_t;
+
+/**
+ * @brief The transport protocols of the sockets that can be looked up.
+ *
+ * The values are the IP protocol numbers, so the protocol field of an IP
+ * header can be passed as is.
+ */
+typedef enum {
+    WS_PROCESS_LOOKUP_TCP = 6,
+    WS_PROCESS_LOOKUP_UDP = 17
+} ws_process_lookup_protocol_t;
+
+/**
+ * @brief One end of a socket: an IPv4 or IPv6 address and a port.
+ */
+typedef struct ws_socket_endpoint {
+    uint8_t  ip_version;      /**< 4 or 6. */
+    union {
+        ws_in4_addr ipv4;     /**< The IPv4 address, in network byte order. */
+        ws_in6_addr ipv6;     /**< The IPv6 address. */
+    } addr;
+    uint16_t port;            /**< The port, in host byte order. */
+} ws_socket_endpoint_t;
+
+/**
+ * @brief A lookup context.
+ *
+ * It holds a snapshot of the operating system's socket tables, refreshed
+ * on demand but not more often than a configurable interval, and a cache
+ * of what is known about the processes found. It is not thread-safe.
+ */
+typedef struct ws_process_lookup ws_process_lookup_t;
+
+/**
+ * @brief Whether the operating system's socket tables can be read on this platform.
+ *
+ * @return true if ws_process_lookup_new() can succeed here.
+ */
+WS_DLL_PUBLIC bool
+ws_process_lookup_supported(void);
+
+/**
+ * @brief Create a lookup context.
+ *
+ * @param err_msg Set to a g_malloc()ed message on failure, if not NULL.
+ * @return The context, to be freed with ws_process_lookup_free(), or NULL
+ * if the platform is not supported or the socket tables cannot be read.
+ */
+WS_DLL_PUBLIC ws_process_lookup_t *
+ws_process_lookup_new(char **err_msg);
+
+/**
+ * @brief Free a lookup context and every ws_process_info_t it returned.
+ *
+ * @param lookup The context; NULL is allowed.
+ */
+WS_DLL_PUBLIC void
+ws_process_lookup_free(ws_process_lookup_t *lookup);
+
+/**
+ * @brief Set how soon the socket tables may be read again after a miss.
+ *
+ * A socket that is not in the snapshot triggers a refresh only if the
+ * previous refresh is at least this old, which bounds the cost of packets
+ * that belong to no local socket. The default is 250 ms.
+ *
+ * @param lookup The context.
+ * @param interval_ms The minimum interval between refreshes, in milliseconds.
+ */
+WS_DLL_PUBLIC void
+ws_process_lookup_set_refresh_interval(ws_process_lookup_t *lookup, unsigned interval_ms);
+
+/**
+ * @brief Read the operating system's socket tables again now.
+ *
+ * @param lookup The context.
+ * @param err_msg Set to a g_malloc()ed message on failure, if not NULL.
+ * @return true on success.
+ */
+WS_DLL_PUBLIC bool
+ws_process_lookup_refresh(ws_process_lookup_t *lookup, char **err_msg);
+
+/**
+ * @brief Find the processes that have a socket open.
+ *
+ * The socket is identified by its local end and, for a connected socket,
+ * its remote end. If no socket matches both, a socket bound to the local
+ * end alone (listening, or an unconnected UDP socket) is looked for, and
+ * then one bound to the local port on any address, of either IP version.
+ * Every process that has a matching socket open is reported: a socket can
+ * be inherited across fork() or passed between processes, and several
+ * sockets can match, e.g. with SO_REUSEPORT. On Windows the system reports
+ * one process per socket, the one that bound it.
+ *
+ * @param lookup The context.
+ * @param protocol The transport protocol.
+ * @param local The end of the socket on this host.
+ * @param remote The other end, or NULL if the socket is not connected or
+ * the other end is unknown.
+ * @param processes Array to which what is known about each process is
+ * appended, as const ws_process_info_t pointers valid until the context
+ * is freed, the process that has had the socket open longest first,
+ * normally the one that created it.
+ * @return The number of processes appended: 0 if no socket matches or
+ * none can be attributed to a process.
+ */
+WS_DLL_PUBLIC unsigned
+ws_process_lookup_socket(ws_process_lookup_t *lookup,
+                         ws_process_lookup_protocol_t protocol,
+                         const ws_socket_endpoint_t *local,
+                         const ws_socket_endpoint_t *remote,
+                         GPtrArray *processes);
+
+/**
+ * @brief Describe a process by its ID.
+ *
+ * @param lookup The context.
+ * @param pid The process ID.
+ * @return What is known about the process, valid until the context is
+ * freed, or NULL if there is no such process.
+ */
+WS_DLL_PUBLIC const ws_process_info_t *
+ws_process_lookup_pid(ws_process_lookup_t *lookup, uint32_t pid);
+
+#ifdef __cplusplus
+}
+#endif /* __cplusplus */
+
+#endif /* __WSUTIL_PROCESS_LOOKUP_H__ */
+
+/*
+ * Editor modelines  -  https://www.wireshark.org/tools/modelines.html
+ *
+ * Local variables:
+ * c-basic-offset: 4
+ * tab-width: 8
+ * indent-tabs-mode: nil
+ * End:
+ *
+ * vi: set shiftwidth=4 tabstop=8 expandtab:
+ * :indentSize=4:tabSize=8:noTabs=true:
+ */

@@ -0,0 +1,96 @@
+/** @file
+ *
+ * The interface between the platform-independent part of the process
+ * lookup and its platform backends. Not installed.
+ *
+ * Wireshark - Network traffic analyzer
+ * By Gerald Combs <gerald@wireshark.org>
+ * Copyright 1998 Gerald Combs
+ *
+ * SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0-or-later
+ */
+
+#ifndef __WSUTIL_PROCESS_LOOKUP_INT_H__
+#define __WSUTIL_PROCESS_LOOKUP_INT_H__
+
+#include "process_lookup.h"
+
+/**
+ * A socket as found in the operating system's tables, in a form that can
+ * be hashed: addresses in network byte order, zero-padded; ports in host
+ * byte order. Always initialize it with ws_process_lookup_key_init(), which
+ * normalizes it: ip_version 0 means the socket is bound to any address (so
+ * it matches both IP versions), and a zero remote address and port mean the
+ * socket is not connected.
+ */
+typedef struct {
+    uint8_t  protocol;
+    uint8_t  ip_version;
+    uint16_t local_port;
+    uint16_t remote_port;
+    uint8_t  local_addr[16];
+    uint8_t  remote_addr[16];
+} ws_process_lookup_socket_key_t;
+
+/**
+ * Initialize a socket key. remote_addr may be NULL. An IPv4 address seen
+ * through an IPv6 socket (::ffff:a.b.c.d) becomes an IPv4 key.
+ */
+void
+ws_process_lookup_key_init(ws_process_lookup_socket_key_t *key,
+                           uint8_t protocol, uint8_t ip_version,
+                           const uint8_t *local_addr, uint16_t local_port,
+                           const uint8_t *remote_addr, uint16_t remote_port);
+
+/**
+ * Called by a backend for each process that has a socket open. It may be
+ * called for several processes with the same socket, and more than once
+ * for the same process and socket.
+ */
+typedef void (*ws_process_lookup_add_socket_func)(void *ctx,
+                                                  const ws_process_lookup_socket_key_t *key,
+                                                  uint32_t pid);
+
+/**
+ * A platform backend. err_msg arguments are never NULL; a message stored
+ * there must be g_malloc()ed.
+ */
+typedef struct {
+    /** Whether this platform is supported at all. */
+    bool supported;
+
+    /** Set up the per-context state; NULL, with *err_msg set, on failure. */
+    void *(*create)(char **err_msg);
+
+    /** Free the per-context state. */
+    void (*destroy)(void *state);
+
+    /** Report every socket that has an owning process, through add(). */
+    bool (*refresh)(void *state, ws_process_lookup_add_socket_func add,
+                    void *ctx, char **err_msg);
+
+    /**
+     * Fill in what is known about a process; info->pid is set on entry and
+     * the rest is zero. The strings must be g_malloc()ed. Returns false if
+     * there is no such process.
+     */
+    bool (*describe)(void *state, uint32_t pid, ws_process_info_t *info);
+} ws_process_lookup_backend_t;
+
+/** The backend for this platform. */
+extern const ws_process_lookup_backend_t ws_process_lookup_backend;
+
+#endif /* __WSUTIL_PROCESS_LOOKUP_INT_H__ */
+
+/*
+ * Editor modelines  -  https://www.wireshark.org/tools/modelines.html
+ *
+ * Local variables:
+ * c-basic-offset: 4
+ * tab-width: 8
+ * indent-tabs-mode: nil
+ * End:
+ *
+ * vi: set shiftwidth=4 tabstop=8 expandtab:

commits_data.title: wsutil: Add a lookup of the processes that have a socket open
commits_data.message:
wsutil: Add a lookup of the processes that have a socket open

Add wsutil/process_lookup.h, which finds the processes that have a TCP
or UDP socket open, given its local and, if connected, remote endpoint,
from the operating system's socket tables, and describes them: name,
executable path, command line, parent process ID, user ID and name, and
start time, the attributes of a pcapng process information block. A
lookup context holds a snapshot of the tables, refreshed when a socket
is not found but not more often than a configurable interval, and a
cache of the processes found, which notices when a process ID is reused
by comparing start times. A socket that is not connected, or listening,
is matched by its local endpoint alone, and one bound to any address by
its port.

Every process that has the socket open is reported, the one that has had
it longest first, since a socket can be inherited across fork() or passed
between processes, and the pcapng epb_processid_threadid option may now
appear once per process.

The backends read what the platform offers to an unprivileged process:
on Windows the IP Helper TCP and UDP tables with owning process IDs, a
Toolhelp snapshot for names and parents, and the process's own memory for
its command line; on Linux /proc/net/{tcp,udp}{,6} and the socket inodes
in /proc/<pid>/fd, and the process's /proc files. Other platforms report
that the lookup is not supported.

This is for dumpcap to record which process sent or received a packet;
nothing uses it yet.

Add unit tests that create sockets and look up the test process itself.

Related to #1184 and #17525.
